evidence.excerpt: This is central to the paper's core contribution (the two-stage strategy) and should be documented (task, masks, class definitions, sample images, statistics), otherwise the mechanism by which Stage I helps is unsupported.

judge_panel.reason: The paper only briefly describes Stage-I as using "an alloy-microstructure dataset [34] as an intermediate domain" that "exposes the model to real metallic texture and microstructural patterns," but provides no documentation of segmentation targets, mask definitions, class labels, sample images, or dataset statistics for Stage-I, leaving the mechanism underspecified.

The Stage-I description is minimal: "For Stage-I adaptation, we use an alloy-microstructure dataset [34] as an intermediate domain between natural images and AM defect data" and "Although not AM-specific, this dataset exposes the model to real metallic texture and microstructural patterns before final adaptation to AM XCT defects." The paper does not specify the Stage-I segmentation targets, masks, or class definitions, so this core step is underdocumented.

While Section IV.D mentions that Stage 1 performs "intermediate domain adaptation on the alloy dataset [34]," it never describes the segmentation targets or masks used to fine-tune the model on this data.

general.reason: For NIST, the paper explicitly says, "Since manually annotated ground-truth defect masks are not publicly available, we generate threshold-derived binary reference masks following the image-processing pipeline of [33]." Yet Sec. IV-E concludes, without that caveat, that "on the real NIST benchmark, XCT-SAM achieves the best IoU and Dice scores among all baselines," so the headline interpretation is not prominently framed as agreement with threshold-derived references.

evidence.excerpt: The conclusions in Sec. IV-E ("XCT-SAM achieves the best IoU and Dice scores among all baselines" on NIST) should be explicitly framed as agreement with threshold-derived reference masks.

judge_panel.reason: The paper states "fine-tuning only 4.15M parameters, or 0.647% of the full model" and trains "two independent binary segmentation models, dedicated to pore and inclusion detection," but never clarifies that the full deployed system requires two such models (~8.3M trainable parameters total), making the efficiency claim potentially misleading.

The paper states, "we train two independent binary segmentation models, dedicated to pore and inclusion detection, respectively," but its efficiency claim is presented as "fine-tuning only 4.15M parameters, or 0.647% of the full model." No passage clarifies that this 4.15M figure is per binary model rather than for the full two-model defect-segmentation system.

The Abstract and Introduction claim the model trains "approximately 4.15M parameters," but Section III.A states that the framework involves training "two independent binary segmentation models," meaning the total trainable parameter count for the full deployment system is not made explicitly clear in the headline metrics.
